passage:
My thumb still twitches, Ayesha, that's how bad it got. I'm Kavitha, and last month I glanced at my phone every couple of minutes, in class, at dinner, even in the bathroom. Because what if the group planned something and I missed it?
Then Amma took the phone for the evening at my aunt's wedding, and I sat there itching, sure the whole world was moving on without me. Nobody moved on. Honestly, nobody even messaged.
The next week I turned off every notification except calls, and I told you, just ring me if it's something real. Remember our trip to the bookshop? I didn't check once 🙂. My heart felt calm for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: Where was Kavitha when Amma took the phone for the evening?
qa.a: Kavitha was at an aunt's wedding.

qa.q: What was Kavitha afraid of while checking the phone so often?
qa.a: Kavitha was afraid the group might plan something that would be missed, feeling sure the whole world was moving on.

qa.q: What did Kavitha change that helped, and what else could Kavitha try?
qa.a: Kavitha turned off every notification except calls and asked Ayesha to ring if something was real; Kavitha could also keep meeting friends offline, as at the bookshop.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt about the request to ring if it's something real?
qa.a: Ayesha probably felt trusted and glad, since it gave a simple way to stay connected and showed the friendship mattered more than the chat.

grounding: Shows a teen checking the phone constantly from fear of missing out, then muting notifications and meeting offline.

passage:
You asked what changed for me this year? Okay, it's going to sound silly. I'm Santosh, and I used to check my phone every three minutes.

Not joking. In class, under the desk. At dinner. In the bathroom. The group chat never stopped, and I was terrified of missing a joke or a plan. If I came back and there were eighty messages I hadn't seen, my chest would go tight, like I'd been left out of my own life.

The day it hit me was at cricket. Abhinav hit the ball straight to me at mid-on and I was looking at my phone. I dropped the easiest catch of the season. Everyone groaned.

That night I turned off notifications for every group. I check twice a day now. Morning, evening. I was scared I'd miss everything.

I didn't. The important stuff, people call. And on Sundays Abhinav and I just go to the ground, phones in the bag. I actually catch things now.

qa.q: How often did Santosh check the phone?
qa.a: Santosh checked the phone every three minutes.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel on coming back to eighty unread messages?
qa.a: Santosh felt anxious and left out, with a tight chest, afraid of missing out on everything.

qa.q: What did Santosh change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Santosh turned off group notifications, checked twice a day and met Abhinav offline, which eased the anxious pull and brought real time with friends.

qa.q: What might Abhinav have felt when the easy catch was dropped?
qa.a: Abhinav probably felt frustrated and let down, since the catch was the easiest of the season.

grounding: It shows a teen who checks the phone every few minutes so as not to miss anything, noticing the anxious pull, turning off notifications and meeting friends offline.

passage:
Sunday. At her cousin's birthday lunch, Gurleen checked her phone eleven times before the cake. The class group was planning something and she couldn't bear to miss it. Her mother tapped the table. "Gurleen. Food." She ate without tasting anything, one eye on the screen.

Wednesday. Gurleen woke up at 1 a.m. to check if anyone had replied to her message. Nobody had. She lay awake, heart thudding, wondering if they were talking without her. In the morning she was so tired she snapped at her little brother. On the bus she thought: I'm scared all the time of missing things. And I'm missing everything that's actually here.

Saturday. She turned off notifications for the class group and two others. It felt like jumping off a ledge. Then she messaged Wasim directly: "Library and then golgappe?" He replied "YES." They spent three hours out. When she checked her phone at home, there were ninety messages. She'd missed nothing that mattered.

qa.q: How many times did Gurleen check her phone before the cake?
qa.a: She checked it eleven times before the cake.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she woke at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: Gurleen felt anxious and afraid of being left out, her heart thudding as she wondered if others were talking without her.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do on Saturday, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Gurleen turned off notifications and met Wasim in person, which eased her fear of missing out and gave her real time with a friend.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's mother feel at the birthday lunch?
qa.a: Her mother likely felt frustrated and a bit worried to see Gurleen so pulled by her phone at a family meal.

grounding: It shows a teen who checks her phone constantly out of fear of missing out, noticing the anxious pull, turning off notifications and meeting a friend offline.
